title: Advanced Reading Comprehension — Long Passages
tagline: Year 3 — Reading 150–250 word passages for structure, detail, inference, tone and vocabulary under time pressure

introduction.overview: Advanced reading comprehension tests whether you can follow an argument across a long passage, not just locate a sentence. Each passage has a structure (a claim, support, a qualification and a conclusion), and each question targets a part of it: the main idea, a stated detail, an implication, the author's attitude, or the meaning of a word in context. Reading with the structure in mind makes questions quick to answer and wrong options easy to spot.
introduction.placementRelevance: Passages of 150–250 words with 5–7 questions are standard in company and campus verbal sections.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading reports, policy notes and emails and extracting what matters is the same skill.

learningObjectives: Read for structure: claim, support, qualification, conclusion
Answer "not mentioned" and "except" questions by elimination
Judge the author's attitude from word choice

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: The main idea is what the whole passage is about; a detail is a single fact. Wrong options are often true statements that are too narrow, too broad or not in the passage.

coreDefinitions: Main idea: the central point the whole passage supports.
Detail question: asks for a fact stated in the passage.
Inference: a conclusion the passage supports but does not state.
Tone: the author's attitude, shown by word choice (cautious, critical, enthusiastic).
Out of scope: an option that may be true in life but is not supported by the passage.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A good passage has a skeleton. Find the sentence that states the claim and the sentence that qualifies it ("though", "but", "yet"); most questions are about those two.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: First pass: one line per paragraph. Second pass: go to the lines that the question points to. Check each option against the passage; reject the extreme, the narrow and the unsupported.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Main idea test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Does the option cover the whole passage?
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Too narrow or too broad: reject

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Detail test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Find the line; paraphrase is allowed

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Inference test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Would the passage lose sense if this were false?

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Except test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Three options are in the text; one is not

mainNarrative: In the heat-island passage, the claim is that cities are warmer than the countryside because of many combined factors. The support is the list of causes and consequences. The qualification is in the last sentence: remedies work best across whole neighbourhoods. The main idea therefore covers causes, effects and remedies, not just one of them.

For a detail question, find the exact sentence. "Hot nights prevent the body from recovering after a hot day, which raises the risk of illness among the elderly" answers a question on why hot nights are harmful.

An inference must be supported, not merely possible. Since the passage says cool roofs work best across whole neighbourhoods, painting one house is likely to have a limited effect on the temperature of the area.
A "NOT mentioned" question is solved by eliminating the three options that appear in the passage. Dark roofs, a lack of trees and vehicle heat are all stated; increased rainfall over cities is not.
Tone shows in the qualifiers. "Early results suggest" and "can lower" are hedged words, so the author is cautiously optimistic about the remedies.

deepDiveAspects.title: Too narrow, too broad
deepDiveAspects.content: A main-idea option that covers only one paragraph is too narrow; one that goes beyond the passage is too broad.

deepDiveAspects.title: Analogies in passages
deepDiveAspects.content: When an author uses an analogy (a farm with one pollinator is like an economy with one industry), the question usually asks what the analogy is meant to show.

solvedExamples.title: Main idea
solvedExamples.question: A passage describes why cities are warmer than the countryside, what harm this causes, and how some cities are responding. What is its main idea?

steps.title: Scope
steps.explanation: The passage covers all three parts.

steps.title: Choose
steps.explanation: The option that covers all three.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: The causes, effects and possible remedies of the urban heat island effect
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: An option about only one part is too narrow.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing an option about air conditioners alone.

solvedExamples.title: Inference
solvedExamples.question: The passage says cool roofs work best across whole neighbourhoods. What can be inferred about painting a single house with light colours?

steps.title: Stated
steps.explanation: The measures work best when applied widely.

steps.title: Implied
steps.explanation: One house is unlikely to change the neighbourhood much.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: It is likely to have only a limited effect on the neighbourhood temperature
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The passage does not call it useless.

solvedExamples.title: Tone
solvedExamples.question: The passage says "early results suggest" that remedies "can lower" temperatures. What is the author's attitude?

shortcutMethods.title: Skeleton first

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Mark the claim, the support and the qualification; answer detail questions from the line, inference questions from the qualification, and tone from the qualifiers.

rulesForApplication: Reject too narrow or too broad.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a true but irrelevant option
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check the passage, not general knowledge.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options with absolute words unless the passage uses them.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Do vocabulary-in-context questions first; they are quick.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Every wrong option fails on scope, support or direction.

easy.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Cities are usually several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a pattern known as the urban heat island effect. The cause is not a single factor but a combination. Dark roofs and roads absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, so the air does not cool as it does over open land. Concrete and glass trap heat between tall buildings, and the lack of trees removes the shade and the moisture that plants normally release. Vehicles, air conditioners and factories add heat of their own. The consequences go beyond discomfort. Hot nights prevent the body from recovering after a hot day, which raises the risk of illness among the elderly. Demand for electricity rises sharply, and the power stations that supply it release more heat and pollution. Some cities have begun to respond with cool roofs painted in light colours, parks, and rules that require new buildings to include green space. Early results suggest that such measures can lower local temperatures by a few degrees, though they work best when applied across whole neighbourhoods rather than on single buildings.

The passage is mainly about
options: the harmful effects of air conditioners in cities
the causes, effects and possible remedies of the urban heat island effect
why the countryside is cooler than it should be
how electricity is generated for big cities
easy.correctAnswer: the causes, effects and possible remedies of the urban heat island effect
easy.explanation: The passage lists causes (dark surfaces, trapped heat, lack of trees), consequences (health, electricity) and remedies (cool roofs, parks). The other options each cover only a fragment.

advanced.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Although honeybees receive most of the attention, many crops depend on wild pollinators such as bumblebees, hoverflies and solitary bees. Farmers who rely only on hired honeybee hives can find that fruit set is poor in cold or wet weather, when honeybees stay indoors but bumblebees keep working. Wild pollinators need nesting sites and a steady supply of flowers, both of which shrink when field margins are cleared and hedgerows removed. Studies on orchards have found that fields bordered by wild flowers receive more visits from pollinators and produce more evenly shaped fruit. The lesson is not that hired hives are useless; they remain valuable at times of peak bloom. It is that a farm with only one pollinator is as vulnerable as an economy with only one industry. Preserving a margin of wild habitat costs the farmer a little land but works like insurance against a bad season.

Which of the following would the author most likely recommend to an orchard owner?
options: Replace hired hives with wild bumblebees entirely
Clear hedgerows to make room for more trees
Leave a margin of wild flowers around the fields while still hiring hives at peak bloom
Avoid hiring hives in cold weather
advanced.correctAnswer: Leave a margin of wild flowers around the fields while still hiring hives at peak bloom
advanced.explanation: The author says hired hives remain valuable at peak bloom and that preserving wild habitat works like insurance, so both together fit best.

advanced.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Few people now write by hand for more than a signature or a shopping list, and the loss is rarely mourned. Typing is faster, and a typed page is easier to read, edit and share. Yet some researchers argue that we pay a hidden price. In experiments, students who took lecture notes by hand remembered concepts better than those who typed, apparently because the slowness of handwriting forces the writer to choose and summarise instead of recording every word. Typists tend to copy, and copying does not require understanding. This does not mean that schools should abandon keyboards. It suggests that the tool should suit the task: a keyboard for drafts that will be revised many times, a pen for material that must be understood and remembered. The danger lies in choosing a tool by habit rather than by purpose.

Which of the following statements is best supported by the passage?
options: Handwriting is always faster than typing
Copying words does not require the writer to understand them
Typed pages are harder to edit
Researchers have proved that typing harms memory
advanced.correctAnswer: Copying words does not require the writer to understand them
advanced.explanation: The passage says typists tend to copy and "copying does not require understanding".

The phrase "works like insurance" in the passage implies that preserving wild habitat
